content:
A gift registry gives supporters a way to buy the equipment your church has selected. A nonprofit Giving List can bring items from different stores together behind a shared link.

Start with your equipment plan and keep a separate record of gifts actually received. The registry helps donors shop; your church still needs to acknowledge donated property accurately.

---

## Start with approved needs

Use your existing equipment plan to decide what belongs on the list. Distinguish essentials from optional additions, and keep purchases aligned with the approved budget. Work through equipment choices before inviting donors to shop.

The portable-equipment guide covers venue needs, team capabilities, storage and purchasing priorities. Carry those decisions into the registry.

<Callout type="tip">
Put an approved item on the list only after you can identify the product and quantity you want. Use item notes to explain details that a donor might otherwise have to guess.
</Callout>

---

## Choose and name your list

MyRegistry offers an organization/nonprofit Giving List and supports adding items from different retailers. It is the worked example in this guide. If you choose another provider, check its own instructions for the same steps.

Create the list using your organization's name. MyRegistry also allows a chapter name, which may help distinguish your plant from another part of a sending church or network. Customize the list with your church's logo and a welcome message explaining the equipment request.

<Callout type="important">
Provider features and IRS guidance were checked October 16, 2026. Before sharing your list, confirm current nonprofit account options, privacy settings and purchase tracking with MyRegistry. Check the current acknowledgment rules in IRS Publication 1771 before issuing receipts.
</Callout>

---

## Make each item specific

With MyRegistry's browser button, you can add an item while viewing its retailer page. Review the title, image, price and quantity in the add-item panel. Add instructions in the item's note field.

Use these fields to make your request clear:

- Confirm that the product matches the item in your equipment plan.
- Set the requested quantity to match your current need.
- Put details such as the selected size or version in the item note.
- Group related needs into categories so donors can browse.
- Favorite the items you most want donors to see as priorities.

MyRegistry supports categories and favorites. Give those tools a purpose, such as grouping storage items together or highlighting an essential item. Keep the details in the item note consistent with the retailer listing.

---

## Check delivery and address visibility

For MyRegistry purchases, donors enter the recipient's address at the retailer's checkout. The shipping information on the list helps them find that address. Check it before you distribute the link.

MyRegistry's privacy statement says your address is visible to people with access to your gift list. It also lets you password-protect the list and make the address private. With a private address, a donor enters a delivery address or requests yours by email. Decide which delivery address your church is comfortable sharing before you send the link.

<Callout type="warning">
Do not assume the registry completes shipping details for the donor. Ask donors to check the recipient and delivery address at the retailer's checkout.
</Callout>

---

## Share the list with instructions

MyRegistry lets nonprofits share their Giving List by email, on a website and through social media. It also offers a website embed. Choose the sharing method that fits how you already communicate with supporters.

Use the welcome message to explain the request, then give donors the list link. Include instructions about the delivery address and marking purchases. For example, ask them to check the item details, use the listed recipient address and confirm the gift's purchase status.

Keep this message about the requested items. Use the church's donor-receipt process to answer acknowledgment questions.

---

## Track purchases and arrivals

A purchase marking and a delivered gift are different events. MyRegistry lets you mark a gift manually when a donor forgets, and restore an item that was marked purchased. Check with the donor before changing a disputed entry.

Use the Thank You Note Tracker to help identify gifts and prepare thanks. Match that information with what your church receives before acknowledging the property. If a gift has not arrived, contact the retailer with the donor's purchase details; MyRegistry stores purchase information under the gift's details.

The retailer handles returns and exchanges. Keep those questions with the store that sold the item, and update the registry when an item needs to become available again.

---

## Acknowledge equipment as property

Under the U.S. federal rule in Publication 1771, a donor needs a contemporaneous written acknowledgment to claim a deduction for a single noncash contribution valued at $250 or more. Additional substantiation requirements may apply.

Use the receiving church's name, describe the donated item and record its receipt date. Describe property without assigning its tax value. If the church provided no goods or services in return, say so; if it provided a benefit, follow the applicable wording in the donor-receipts guide.

The donor handles the valuation used on their return. Keep an equipment gift separate from monetary gift totals, consistent with the published donor-receipts guide. Use the church's acknowledgment process even when the registry has already helped you send a thank-you.

---

## Review before sending the link

- [ ] Match listed items to the approved equipment plan.
- [ ] Check product details, quantities and notes.
- [ ] Organize the list and identify priority items.
- [ ] Review the recipient address and its visibility to donors.
- [ ] Explain how donors should mark a purchase.
- [ ] Plan to compare purchase records with actual arrivals.
- [ ] Use the church's property-gift acknowledgment process.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"In this case, moreover, it is required of stewards that one be found faithful."* — 1 Corinthians 4:2 (LSB)
</Callout>
excerpt: Build an equipment gift list, guide donors through purchases and delivery, and acknowledge donated items accurately.
title: Using a Gift Registry for Equipment

sources.claim: Published context for opening paragraphs, approved equipment plan, section 1, receipt date and separation from monetary totals in section 7, and final checklist. Local seed opened and nearest articles read in full: Acquiring Portable Church Equipment; Donor Receipts and Giving Statements; Designated Giving Policies; Disbursements and Approvals. Practical instructions apply those existing guides; no new church policy.
sources.quote: Expenditures should align with the approved budget. […] Distinguish between essential and optional […] For donated equipment, acknowledge the item and receipt date

sources.claim: Opening and section 2: organization/nonprofit list, organization and chapter naming, multiple retailers, logo and welcome message. Editorial example of naming a plant within a sending organization; no provider endorsement. Opened with curl after browser fetch timed out.
sources.quote: Input your Organization Name and if you have one, your chapter name. […] add your logo […] Create a welcome page

sources.claim: Opening and section 2: products from online stores, offline gifts and a shared link. This guide selects physical items and does not describe or price cash funds.
sources.quote: Start adding gifts from any store […] Adding products from online stores […] share your registry with friends and family using one simple link.

sources.claim: Section 3: browser-button item addition, confirming title/image/price/quantity; item list and checklist apply the fields to approved equipment. No automatic accuracy or availability guarantee.
sources.quote: A window will appear in the top-right corner, allowing you to confirm the item’s price, title, image, and quantity.

sources.claim: Section 1 tip, section 3 and sharing instructions: item notes can carry instructions, selected sizes or versions. Those are editorial examples of details to put in supported note fields.
sources.quote: Here you can add any instructions, details, or personal notes for your guests about that item.

sources.claim: Section 3 and final checklist: categories help donors browse; storage is an editorial example, not an imposed church equipment taxonomy.
sources.quote: You can organize items into categories to make your registry easier for guests to browse.

sources.claim: Section 3 item list and final checklist: favorite desired items to signal priorities; no claim about automatic sorting.
sources.quote: You can inform your guests about your most desired items by favoriting the gift!

sources.claim: Section 4, warning and invitation instructions: donor enters recipient address at retailer checkout; list shipping information contains address. Review recipient/address is practical application, not a claim of automatic transfer.
sources.quote: They simply enter the registrant’s shipping address in the shipping section at checkout. […] under the shipping info section.

sources.claim: Section 4 and final checklist: gift-list addresses are visible to people with list access, with options to password-protect the list and make the address private. With a private address, donors enter a delivery address or request it from the list owner by email. Check which address the church is comfortable sharing before publishing the link.
sources.quote: Please be aware that your address will be visible to individuals who have access to your gift list. Members have the option to protect their gift list with a password and to control the visibility of their address on the gift list.

sources.claim: Section 5: nonprofits can share by email, website or social media and embed the list. Choice of church communication channel is editorial application.
sources.quote: through email, their website, social media, and other messaging platforms. […] select Embed Your Giving List on Your Website

sources.claim: Section 6 and donor instructions: manual purchase marking is possible when a donor omits it; no automatic duplicate-prevention guarantee.
sources.quote: The registrant can manually mark the gift as purchased to prevent duplicate gifts.

sources.claim: Section 6: a marked purchase can be reversed. Checking with a donor before changing disputed status is editorial application of this capability.
sources.quote: Yes. You can unmark an item as purchased so it becomes available again.

sources.claim: Section 6 and final checklist: thank-you tracking exists. Comparing its entries with actual arrivals is a workflow recommendation, not a claim that a tracker certifies delivery or issues a valid tax acknowledgment.
sources.quote: Yes. MyRegistry.com provides a thank-you tracker.

sources.claim: Section 6: retailer handles undelivered order tracking; purchase details are stored under gift information. Paired with manual purchase marking, supports distinguishing purchased from actually received.
sources.quote: you will need to contact the store where the item was bought. […] The details are stored under the gift

sources.claim: Section 6: retailer handles returns and exchanges. Registry restoration is sourced separately; no return window or universal return desk is promised.
sources.quote: Returns and exchanges are handled by the retailer where the gift was purchased.

sources.claim: Section 7: Publication 1771, pages 3–4, donor’s contemporaneous acknowledgment for single noncash contribution valued at $250 or more; receiving organization name; additional substantiation may apply. Important callout checks current rules. Not a charity penalty claim or a guarantee of deductibility.
sources.quote: single noncash contribution valued at $250 or more […] the name of the organization […] Additional substantiation requirements may apply to noncash contributions.

sources.claim: Section 7: describe property without its tax value; state no return goods/services only if true. Any return benefit uses the published donor-receipts guide, not a blanket template.
sources.quote: description (but not value) of non-cash contribution; […] statement that no goods or services were provided by the organization, if that is the case;

sources.claim: Section 7: valuation on the donor’s tax return is the donor’s responsibility; church does not turn list price into a deductible amount. No appraisal thresholds or form instructions are supplied.
sources.quote: Supporting the FMV listed on your return is your responsibility.

sources.claim: Scripture callout only. Opened exactly 1 Corinthians 4:2 on the LSB site with curl; read the single verse text in returned page. No interpretation or new theology ruling.
sources.publisher: The Lockman Foundation / Three Sixteen Publishing
sources.quote: In this case, moreover, it is required of stewards that one be found faithful.

claim_check.notes: Author source mapping only; independent Opus claim, one-verse scripture and full desktop/mobile screenshot review required. Sources accessed 2026-10-16. No state examples. Procedural recommendations apply cited provider capabilities and the named published guides; they do not create legal duties. Source quotes are short exact excerpts; […] separates excerpts. Volatile provider options and federal rules are explicitly dated in the body. Author-only excerpt verification passed for all 19 source entries after normalizing PDF line-end hyphenation and removing LSB footnote markup. This checks quotation accuracy, not independent claim approval. Author rendered desktop and mobile, checked every section, item list, checklist and full LSB footer. Lint has only the exact-scripture word “moreover” warning.

rulings: Resolved editorial choice: keep A20 as the assigned separate registry how-to and link the existing equipment guide; do not duplicate its purchasing plan.
Resolved editorial choice: MyRegistry nonprofit Giving List is a worked example, not a preferred-provider claim; omit price, fee, discount and deadline promises.

Resolved scope: focus on physical equipment gifts. Exclude cash funds, gift cards, large-gift appraisal/form thresholds, resale reporting and state-tax examples; those need separate transaction-specific review.
Resolved consistency: donated equipment remains property, acknowledged without church-assigned tax value and separate from monetary totals, matching the published donor-receipts article.
No open theology, pastoral-care or methodology rulings. Scripture is reproduced without an interpretive application.
